title: Singles Marriage Readiness Assessment
changeLog: v3 Final: Scenario-based questions, non-linear scoring, relatable outcome signals, gender-aware insights with 4-way personalization, 4-phase narrative ordering.

STRONG.title: A Solid Foundation
STRONG.summary: You've done the deep work that most people skip. The emotional health, relational maturity, and spiritual grounding reflected in your answers aren't things that happen by accident; they're the fruit of intention, honesty, and probably some hard seasons you chose to grow through instead of just survive. You're not perfect, and you know that. But you've built something real inside yourself: the kind of foundation that can hold the weight of covenant love. Marriage will still stretch you; it's meant to. But you're entering from a place of wholeness, not desperation. That matters more than most people realize.

genderTitle.male: A Man Ready to Lead and Love Well

genderSummary.male: Brother, what stands out in your answers is something rare: you've done the interior work. You're not chasing marriage to fill a void or prove something to yourself. You've dealt with your wounds honestly, you've built emotional intelligence that most men avoid, and your faith isn't theoretical — it's load-bearing. The woman who marries you will be stepping into something secure. Not because you have it all figured out, but because you've shown the willingness to look at yourself clearly, own what you find, and keep growing. That's the kind of man who can lead a home — not with control, but with the quiet strength that comes from a man who knows who he is in God.
genderSummary.female: Sister, your answers reveal something beautiful: you're not waiting for marriage to complete you — you've been doing that inner work already. You've wrestled with your own patterns, built genuine emotional security, and cultivated a faith that goes deeper than Sunday attendance. The man who steps into your life will find a woman who knows her worth, who can communicate with clarity, and who brings spiritual depth into the relationship — not because she's performing, but because it's who she's become. You're not desperate. You're ready. And there's a profound difference.

STRONG.narrativeFrame: This result doesn't mean marriage will be easy. It means you've built the kind of interior life that can weather what marriage actually requires. The patterns you've developed in how you handle conflict, manage your emotions, connect with God, and relate to others aren't just good habits; they're the architecture of a healthy marriage. Keep growing. Stay humble. But walk forward with confidence: the foundation beneath you is real.

DEVELOPING.title: Real Progress, Clear Next Steps
DEVELOPING.summary: Here's what's true: you're not starting from scratch. There's genuine health in several areas of your life. Real strength showed up in your answers. You're building something good. But honesty matters here, so let's name it plainly: there are specific areas where you're still growing into the kind of person who can sustain a covenant marriage. That's not a failure; it's an invitation. The gap between where you are and where you need to be isn't a wall; it's a doorway. You're closer than you think, but the work ahead is specific, not vague. You don't need to overhaul your life. You need to focus.

genderTitle.male: A Man on the Right Path with Work Still Ahead
genderTitle.female: A Woman Growing into Her Readiness

genderSummary.male: You're not the man who hasn't thought about any of this — and that matters. You've got areas of genuine strength: maybe your faith is steady, or you handle conflict better than most, or you've started dealing with old wounds. That's real. But here's what came through in your answers: there are places where your emotional maturity, relational skills, or spiritual consistency haven't caught up with your desire for marriage. Maybe you avoid hard conversations, or you haven't fully dealt with patterns from your family of origin, or your sense of identity still shifts too easily. None of this disqualifies you. But a wife deserves a man who's done this work — not perfectly, but honestly. The growth ahead of you isn't optional if you want a marriage that lasts. It's the next chapter of becoming the man God is shaping you into.
genderSummary.female: There's real strength in what you shared — don't overlook that. Some of your answers reflect genuine emotional health, spiritual depth, or relational wisdom that you've clearly been cultivating. But woven through your responses are areas where the readiness isn't fully there yet. Maybe it's a pattern of emotional dependency, or boundaries that blur under pressure, or a faith life that's more reactive than rooted. Perhaps you haven't fully grieved something from your past, or your expectations of marriage carry weight that marriage itself was never meant to hold. None of this means you're broken. It means you're in process — and that process matters. The woman who walks into marriage having done this specific work will build something vastly different than the one who skips it.

DEVELOPING.narrativeFrame: You're in a season where intentional growth can change everything. The areas that need attention aren't mysteries. They showed up clearly in your answers, and that's actually a gift. Most people walk into marriage unaware of their gaps. You're aware. Now the question is whether you'll treat that awareness as information or as an invitation to do something about it. Find a mentor, a counselor, a small group, a spiritual director, someone who can walk with you into the specific areas that surfaced here. Six months of focused growth in those places could shift your entire trajectory.

GUARDED.title: Important Areas Need Honest Attention
GUARDED.summary: This is a result that requires courage to sit with, and that courage is itself a sign of something good in you. The patterns that showed up across your answers point to real areas of unresolved pain, relational immaturity, or spiritual disconnection that would create serious difficulty in a marriage. This isn't said to shame you; it's said because marriage is a pressure system, and whatever isn't healed gets amplified under that pressure. Right now, stepping into marriage would mean bringing unprocessed wounds, undeveloped skills, or an unstable foundation into the most demanding relationship of your life. You deserve better than that. So does the person you'd marry.

genderTitle.male: A Man with Real Work to Do Before He's Ready
genderTitle.female: A Woman Who Needs to Heal Before She Commits

genderSummary.male: This is hard to hear, and I'm not going to soften it with platitudes: your answers reveal significant areas where you're not yet ready to be the man a wife needs you to be. That might be unresolved anger, emotional unavailability, patterns of avoidance, a shaky sense of identity, or a faith that hasn't been tested enough to anchor a family. Maybe it's several of those. This doesn't mean God has written you off or that marriage isn't in your future. It means that the man you are today would struggle deeply in marriage — and the fallout from that wouldn't just hurt you. There is a version of you that's ready for this. But he requires some honest, probably uncomfortable work to uncover. A counselor, a pastor who won't just tell you what you want to hear, a men's group with real accountability — these aren't optional. They're the bridge between where you are and where you need to be.
genderSummary.female: What your answers reveal isn't easy to read, but you deserve the truth: there are significant areas in your emotional health, relational patterns, or spiritual life that aren't ready to bear the weight of marriage. Maybe you've been carrying pain you haven't processed — from your family, from past relationships, from disappointments you've pushed down instead of worked through. Maybe you've built walls you call boundaries, or you've confused longing for readiness. Marriage would not fix these things. It would expose them. And the exposure would be painful — for you and for the man you'd marry. But here's what's also true: you took this assessment. You answered honestly. That tells me there's a part of you that knows something needs to shift. Listen to that voice. Get into a counseling relationship. Find a mentor or spiritual director who can sit with the hard stuff. The healing you need is available — but it requires you to stop performing and start being honest.

GUARDED.narrativeFrame: This isn't a verdict. It's a guardrail. The fact that these patterns showed up now—before you made a lifelong covenant—is actually grace. Most people discover these issues inside a marriage, when the stakes are highest and the exits are hardest. You have an opportunity right now to address the root causes, not just the symptoms. Don't rush past this result to get to the relationship you want. Sit with it. Let it trouble you enough to act. The marriage you're hoping for will require a version of you that doesn't exist yet, but can.

AT_RISK.title: Pause, Heal, and Rebuild Before Moving Forward
AT_RISK.summary: Please hear this with the gravity and the gentleness it's intended to carry: your answers reveal deep, consistent patterns of unresolved pain, relational dysfunction, or spiritual crisis that make marriage genuinely dangerous for you right now—not as a punishment, but as a reality. Marriage doesn't heal brokenness. It reveals it, magnifies it, and puts it on an accelerated timeline. Entering a covenant relationship in your current state would almost certainly lead to profound suffering—yours and your spouse's. This assessment isn't the final word on your life. But it is an honest mirror. And the most courageous, most loving thing you can do right now—for yourself and for the future person you might marry—is to stop, acknowledge the depth of what you're carrying, and get serious help.

genderTitle.male: A Man Who Needs to Stop and Heal
genderTitle.female: A Woman Who Needs Rescue Before Romance

genderSummary.male: Brother, I need to be straight with you because too many people in your life probably haven't been: you are not ready for marriage. Not close. And rushing toward it in your current state would cause damage — to you, and especially to the woman who'd trust you with her life. Your answers point to deep-seated patterns: maybe severe emotional detachment, unresolved trauma, spiritual abandonment, destructive conflict patterns, or an identity so fractured that you're looking for a wife to give you a sense of self. These aren't flaws to manage — they're wounds to heal. You might be angry reading this. You might want to dismiss it. But if even part of you recognizes the truth in it, that part of you is worth listening to. You need professional help. Not a podcast. Not a self-help book. A licensed counselor, a trauma-informed pastor, and probably a long runway of consistent healing work before marriage should even be a conversation. This isn't the end of your story. But this chapter has to be about getting well — not getting married.
genderSummary.female: Sister, this is going to be the hardest thing you've read today, and I need you to stay with me: your answers reveal a level of pain, dysfunction, or spiritual crisis that makes marriage harmful for you right now. Not inconvenient. Harmful. Maybe you've been carrying trauma you've never fully named. Maybe your relational patterns are shaped by survival — not love. Maybe your sense of self is so tangled in the desire to be chosen that you'd accept things in a marriage that would slowly destroy you. Maybe your faith is in freefall and you're hoping a godly man will stabilize what only God and honest healing can rebuild. Whatever combination your answers reflected, the message is the same: marriage right now would not rescue you. It would put you and your future husband in a situation neither of you is equipped to survive well. Please — get help. Real help. A counselor who specializes in the things you're carrying. A mentor who won't just pray over you but will walk with you into the dark places. A faith community where you can be fully honest and fully loved. You are worth the time this healing will take. And the woman who emerges from that process will be ready for a love that your current self cannot yet hold.

AT_RISK.narrativeFrame: If this result scares you—good. Let it. Fear in this case isn't the enemy; complacency is. Every pattern that showed up in your answers has a root, and every root can be addressed. But not on your own, not quickly, and not while simultaneously trying to pursue marriage. This is a season for radical honesty, professional support, and spiritual rebuilding. It may take a year. It may take longer. But the person who comes out the other side of that process will be someone capable of a marriage that actually works—not a marriage that slowly falls apart under the weight of everything that was never dealt with. God is not done with you. But right now, the invitation isn't toward the altar. It's toward the healing that makes the altar possible.

insights.low: You may struggle with feeling secure in relationships. Building a stronger sense of your own worth and value is foundational for a healthy marriage.
insights.medium: You have a reasonable sense of security but may experience doubt in certain situations. Continuing to build confidence in your emotional foundation strengthens relationships.
insights.high: You feel secure and valued. This emotional foundation allows you to be vulnerable and trusting in marriage, which is essential for intimacy.
insights.microStep: Identify one person you trust deeply and share something meaningful with them this week. Notice how their response affects your sense of security.

genderLow.male: Many men learn to mask insecurity with independence or emotional distance. If you struggle to feel secure, it's often because vulnerability was treated as weakness growing up. Relearning that emotional safety is strength — not softness — changes everything.
genderLow.female: Women often tie their sense of security to how others respond to them. If you find yourself constantly reading the room for signs of rejection, your worth has become dependent on someone else's mood. Building internal security frees you to love without desperation.

genderMedium.male: You have a decent foundation, but you may still default to self-reliance when things get uncertain. Learning to stay emotionally present — rather than going into 'fix it' or 'shut down' mode — will make you a safer partner.
genderMedium.female: You're more secure than many, but doubt may still creep in during silence or distance from someone you care about. Strengthening your internal anchor means you won't need constant reassurance to feel loved.

genderHigh.male: Emotional security in a man creates a safe harbor for his wife. Your steadiness means she can be vulnerable without fear — and that's one of the greatest gifts a husband can give.
genderHigh.female: A woman who feels secure in herself brings peace into a marriage rather than anxiety. Your groundedness means you won't need your husband to constantly prove his love — freeing him to love you freely.

genderMicroStep.male: This week, when you feel the urge to withdraw or 'handle it yourself,' pause and let someone in instead. Practice saying 'I'm struggling with this' to one trusted person.
genderMicroStep.female: This week, when you feel the urge to seek reassurance, pause and sit with the discomfort for 10 minutes first. Journal what you're actually afraid of underneath the anxiety.

insights.low: Conflict may trigger withdrawal, aggression, or avoidance in you. Marriage requires facing disagreements directly. Learning healthy conflict patterns is crucial.
insights.medium: You can handle some conflict but may avoid difficult conversations or escalate tensions. Growing in this area will strengthen your marriage significantly.
insights.high: You approach conflict as a chance to understand your partner better. This perspective creates safety and deepens intimacy even during disagreements.
insights.microStep: Bring up one small concern with someone you trust this week. Practice stating your perspective calmly without blame.

genderLow.male: Men are often socialized to either dominate in conflict or avoid it entirely. If your instinct is to escalate or shut down, you're following a script that will destroy intimacy in marriage.
genderLow.female: Women are often taught that conflict means something is wrong with the relationship. If you avoid hard conversations to 'keep the peace,' you're actually building resentment that will surface later — often explosively.

genderMedium.male: You can engage in conflict, but you may still default to logic-only mode or dismiss your partner's emotional experience as 'overreacting.' Learning to validate before solving is a game-changer.
genderMedium.female: You handle conflict better than most, but you may still struggle with bringing things up directly. Hint-dropping or expecting your partner to 'just know' won't work in marriage.

genderHigh.male: A man who can face conflict calmly and stay engaged without getting defensive makes his wife feel safe enough to be honest. That safety is the foundation of lasting trust.
genderHigh.female: A woman who can address conflict directly without withdrawing or escalating is a rare gift. Your future husband will feel safe to be imperfect around you — and that creates real intimacy.

genderMicroStep.male: This week, when someone disagrees with you, resist the urge to win or withdraw. Instead, ask: 'Help me understand your perspective.' Listen for 60 seconds before responding.
genderMicroStep.female: This week, bring up one small concern directly instead of hinting at it. Use the phrase: 'Something has been on my mind, and I want to share it with you honestly.'

insights.low: You may struggle to move past conflict or rebuild connection after disagreements. Learning repair strategies is key — every marriage has conflict, but healthy marriages recover well.
insights.medium: You can usually patch things up but may not fully rebuild emotional connection. Deepening your repair skills will prevent resentment from building.
insights.high: You know how to repair ruptures, apologize meaningfully, and reconnect after conflict. This skill is one of the strongest predictors of lasting marriage.
insights.microStep: If there's unresolved tension from a recent disagreement, reach out and have a genuine conversation about how both of you felt.

genderLow.male: Many men struggle with repair because apologizing feels like losing. But in marriage, the man who can say 'I was wrong' with no qualifiers is the man whose wife feels safe to stay.
genderLow.female: Women sometimes confuse talking about the conflict with actually repairing it. If you revisit the same hurt repeatedly without resolution, the wound stays open. Learning to close the loop — forgive and move forward — is essential.

genderMedium.male: You can patch things up, but you may rush to 'fix it' without fully understanding the emotional impact. Slowing down to ask 'how did that affect you?' before offering solutions deepens repair.
genderMedium.female: You're good at reconnecting after conflict, but you may hold onto residual hurt longer than you realize. Check whether you've truly let go or just buried it to keep the peace.

genderHigh.male: A man who repairs well is a man who creates emotional safety. Your ability to take ownership and reconnect after rupture is one of the most protective skills in marriage.
genderHigh.female: Your ability to repair and restore connection after conflict is a sign of deep emotional intelligence. Your future husband will feel safe to be human with you — mistakes and all.

genderMicroStep.male: After your next disagreement, initiate repair first — even if you feel the other person was more wrong. Say: 'I don't want this between us. Can we talk about what happened?'
genderMicroStep.female: After your next disagreement, check in with yourself honestly: have you actually forgiven, or are you keeping score? If you're holding onto it, name that to the other person.

insights.low: Your values and priorities may differ significantly from those in your typical circle. Alignment on core life decisions is essential before marriage.
insights.medium: You generally align on important decisions but might differ on some values. Having open conversations about major life choices will help.
insights.high: Your values and priorities align well. Shared vision on finances, faith, family, and life goals creates a strong foundation for marriage.
insights.microStep: Write down your top 5 life priorities. Imagine sharing these with a potential partner and notice which areas feel non-negotiable.

genderLow.male: Men sometimes assume their priorities will naturally align with a partner's — or that their vision should lead by default. Marriage requires genuine collaboration, not just agreement from someone else.
genderLow.female: Women sometimes suppress their own priorities to match a partner's vision. If you can't clearly name your non-negotiables apart from a relationship, you'll lose yourself inside one.

genderMedium.male: You have a general sense of direction, but you may not have pressure-tested your values against real-life trade-offs. What happens when career goals and family goals conflict? Know your answer before marriage.
genderMedium.female: You know what matters to you, but you may be flexible to the point of compromising things that shouldn't be compromised. Knowing where your flexibility ends protects your future marriage.

genderHigh.male: A man who knows his values and can articulate them clearly gives his future wife confidence and security in the direction of their life together.
genderHigh.female: A woman who knows her non-negotiables and can communicate them without apology attracts a partner who respects her — and repels those who would diminish her.

genderMicroStep.male: Write down your top 3 non-negotiable values for marriage (faith, finances, family size, location). Ask yourself: would you walk away from a relationship if these weren't shared?
genderMicroStep.female: Write down 3 values you'd never compromise on — even for someone you love deeply. Practice saying them out loud. Your clarity protects your future.

insights.low: Emotions may feel overwhelming or out of control at times. Marriage amplifies all feelings. Developing emotional management tools is vital before committing.
insights.medium: You manage emotions reasonably well but may lose composure under stress. Building consistency in how you handle big feelings will strengthen relationships.
insights.high: You understand your emotions and can express them constructively. This maturity allows you to navigate marriage's ups and downs with grace.
insights.microStep: The next time you feel strong emotion, pause and name it specifically. Notice where you feel it in your body and what triggered it.

genderLow.male: Men who struggle with emotional regulation often express it as anger, withdrawal, or numbing. These are coping strategies, not strength. Marriage needs a man who can feel without exploding or disappearing.
genderLow.female: Women who struggle with emotional regulation may experience emotional flooding — where everything feels urgent and overwhelming. In marriage, this pattern exhausts both you and your partner. Building regulation skills is an act of self-love.

genderMedium.male: You keep it together most of the time, but stress may push you toward shutting down or snapping. Knowing your early warning signs — and having a plan for them — prevents damage in marriage.
genderMedium.female: You manage emotions well in most situations, but high-stress moments may trigger tears, anxiety, or over-talking. Recognizing what dysregulation looks like for you helps you catch it earlier.

genderHigh.male: A man who can feel deeply and still stay grounded is magnetic. Your emotional steadiness creates a safe environment where your wife can be fully herself.
genderHigh.female: A woman who understands her emotions and expresses them constructively brings clarity instead of chaos to a marriage. Your emotional intelligence is a genuine superpower.

genderMicroStep.male: This week, when frustration or stress rises, name the emotion out loud: 'I'm feeling frustrated.' This simple act engages your brain's reasoning center and slows the reactive pattern.
genderMicroStep.female: This week, when emotions intensify, try the 90-second rule: the chemical surge of any emotion lasts about 90 seconds. Breathe through it, then decide how to respond.

insights.low: Some patterns from your upbringing may still affect how you handle trust and conflict. Noticing them is the first step to building something healthier.
insights.medium: You seem to recognize some patterns from your upbringing and you're learning new ways to respond. With practice, this can become a strong foundation for marriage.
insights.high: Your answers show you can reflect on your upbringing and choose healthier patterns. This supports a stable and emotionally safe marriage.
insights.microStep: Write down one family pattern you don't want to repeat and one healthier response you want to practice this week.

genderLow.male: Many men unconsciously replicate their father's patterns — for better or worse. If your dad was distant, harsh, or absent, those templates are shaping how you'll show up as a husband unless you intentionally rewrite them.
genderLow.female: Women often carry their mother's relational patterns — people-pleasing, over-functioning, or emotional caretaking. Recognizing which patterns are yours by choice versus inherited by default is where freedom begins.

genderMedium.male: You see some of your family's influence, but blind spots remain. Pay attention to how you handle anger, affection, and vulnerability — that's where the inherited patterns hide.
genderMedium.female: You've started recognizing inherited patterns, but some still run on autopilot — especially around conflict, control, or emotional caretaking. Keep digging. The patterns you can't see are the ones that hurt most.

genderHigh.male: A man who has examined his family patterns and made deliberate choices about what to carry forward builds a new legacy. Your future family benefits from every pattern you've consciously chosen.
genderHigh.female: A woman who understands her family's influence and has chosen her own path brings clarity and health into marriage. You're not repeating a cycle — you're starting a new one.

genderMicroStep.male: Ask yourself: 'How did my father handle conflict, affection, and failure?' Then ask: 'Which of those patterns do I want to carry into my marriage?' Write it down.
genderMicroStep.female: Ask yourself: 'What did I learn about love, sacrifice, and worth from watching my mother?' Identify one pattern you want to keep and one you want to release.

insights.low: Stress tends to overwhelm you or lead to unhealthy coping. Marriage involves seasons of real stress — financial, health, relational. Resilience can be built.
insights.medium: You handle typical stress but might struggle with multiple pressures. Expanding your coping toolkit will help you and your spouse weather life's storms.
insights.high: You manage stress well and maintain perspective during hard times. Your stability is a gift to your marriage and your partner.
insights.microStep: Identify two healthy stress-management practices (walk, journal, talk, pray, exercise) and commit to using one this week.

genderLow.male: Men under stress often isolate, overwork, or numb with distractions. Your future wife needs a partner who can say 'I'm struggling' instead of disappearing into the garage or the screen.
genderLow.female: Women under stress often over-function — doing more, carrying more, saying they're 'fine' while burning out. Your future husband needs a partner who can ask for help, not just give it.

genderMedium.male: You manage everyday stress, but crisis-level pressure may push you into old coping patterns — silence, control, or escapism. Building a stress plan now prevents marital damage later.
genderMedium.female: You handle stress reasonably well, but you may absorb other people's stress as your own. Learning to carry your load without carrying everyone else's protects your energy for marriage.

genderHigh.male: A man who stays steady through hard seasons gives his wife and family a sense of security that money and status can never provide. Your resilience is leadership in its purest form.
genderHigh.female: A woman who can weather storms without losing herself is a pillar of strength. Your steadiness in hard seasons will be one of the most trusted qualities in your marriage.

genderMicroStep.male: Identify your go-to stress response (isolate, overwork, numb out). This week, choose one healthy alternative and use it before the old pattern kicks in.
genderMicroStep.female: This week, when you feel the urge to take on someone else's burden, pause and ask: 'Is this mine to carry?' Practice saying 'I care about you, and I also need to take care of myself.'

insights.low: When hurt, you may withdraw, retaliate, or shut down emotionally. Learning to communicate pain without damaging the relationship is essential.
insights.medium: You can express when you're hurt but might need to work on staying connected during those moments. Vulnerability during hurt deepens intimacy.
insights.high: You can share hurt feelings constructively and stay open to your partner's perspective. This openness is rare and invaluable in marriage.
insights.microStep: Next time you're hurt by someone, instead of withdrawing, share honestly: 'I felt hurt when... and here's why it mattered to me.'

genderLow.male: When men are hurt, the most common response is anger or withdrawal — both of which feel safer than admitting pain. But in marriage, a wife needs to know when she's hurt you. Silence is not strength.
genderLow.female: When women are hurt, the response is often to over-explain, pursue relentlessly, or eventually shut down completely. Learning to express hurt clearly and then give space is a skill that protects intimacy.

genderMedium.male: You can share hurt sometimes, but you may minimize it or frame it as frustration instead of pain. Letting your guard down further — saying 'that hurt me' — deepens connection.
genderMedium.female: You express hurt, but you may need to work on timing and delivery. Sharing pain in the heat of the moment versus after reflection can mean the difference between connection and conflict.

genderHigh.male: A man who can say 'that hurt me' without retaliating or shutting down is a man who builds deep trust. Your vulnerability is a gift your future wife will treasure.
genderHigh.female: A woman who can express hurt without attacking or withdrawing creates an environment where both partners feel safe to be imperfect. That safety is the foundation of lasting love.

genderMicroStep.male: Next time someone hurts you, resist the urge to get angry or go silent. Instead, try: 'I need you to know that hurt me. I'm not attacking you — I'm letting you in.'
genderMicroStep.female: Next time you're hurt, wait 30 minutes before responding. Then share with this framework: 'When you did X, I felt Y, because Z matters to me.' Keep it about your experience, not their character.

insights.low: You may be more focused on immediate satisfaction than building something lasting. Consider what long-term stability and commitment mean to you.
insights.medium: You balance present happiness with future goals, though you might sometimes prioritize the now over long-term plans. Clarifying your vision helps guide choices.
insights.high: You naturally think ahead and make choices aligned with long-term goals. This stability helps you build a marriage that thrives through seasons.
insights.microStep: Write down one long-term goal you have for your life and relationship, then identify one action this week to move toward it.

genderLow.male: Men who live for the moment often struggle with the daily discipline marriage requires. Romantic feelings fade — what remains is commitment, purpose, and showing up on ordinary days.
genderLow.female: Women who focus primarily on the present may rush into relationships based on chemistry without evaluating long-term compatibility. Slow down. Marriage is a 50-year decision, not a feeling.

genderMedium.male: You think ahead sometimes, but you may struggle with follow-through when things get boring or costly. Marriage rewards the man who stays consistent, not the one who shows up only when inspired.
genderMedium.female: You balance present and future well, but you may sometimes compromise long-term goals when emotions are high. Grounding decisions in your values — not your feelings — protects your future.

genderHigh.male: A man with long-term vision creates stability and direction for his family. Your ability to delay gratification and stay focused on what matters most is a foundation your marriage will be built on.
genderHigh.female: A woman who thinks long-term and builds with intention brings wisdom and stability into partnership. Your future-oriented mindset means you won't settle for short-term spark over lasting substance.

genderMicroStep.male: Write down where you want your life to be in 10 years — spiritually, financially, relationally. Then ask: does the way I'm living today move me toward or away from that vision?
genderMicroStep.female: Write down 3 qualities that will matter in year 20 of marriage (not year 1). Use that list to evaluate what you prioritize in a partner versus what culture tells you to prioritize.

insights.low: Your expectations may be unrealistic or poorly defined. Unmet expectations are a major source of disappointment. Clarifying your vision prevents disillusionment.
insights.medium: You have a general sense of what marriage should be like but haven't deeply examined your specific expectations. Reflection strengthens your readiness.
insights.high: You have realistic, thoughtful expectations rooted in your values. You understand marriage requires work and grace. This wisdom prevents preventable conflict.
insights.microStep: Write down 5-10 expectations you have for marriage. Circle which are realistic and which might need adjustment.

genderLow.male: Many men enter marriage expecting it to fill a void — for companionship, sex, validation, or purpose. When those expectations meet reality, disillusionment hits hard. Know what marriage actually is before you enter it.
genderLow.female: Many women carry a fairy-tale script for marriage — conscious or not. When the reality of living with an imperfect person replaces the fantasy, the crash is devastating. Examine your expectations honestly.

genderMedium.male: You have a reasonable sense of what marriage involves, but you may underestimate the emotional labor required. Marriage doesn't just need a provider — it needs a partner who is fully present.
genderMedium.female: You have solid expectations generally, but you may still carry some unspoken ones — about romance, leadership, or emotional availability. The expectations you don't voice are the ones that cause the most conflict.

genderHigh.male: A man who enters marriage with clear, realistic expectations sets the stage for gratitude rather than disappointment. Your grounded perspective protects your marriage from preventable conflict.
genderHigh.female: A woman with healthy, examined expectations is positioned to appreciate her husband for who he is — not resent him for who he isn't. This clarity is a gift to both of you.

genderMicroStep.male: Talk to a married man you respect and ask: 'What surprised you most about marriage? What do you wish you'd known?' Let his answers adjust your expectations.
genderMicroStep.female: Talk to a married woman you respect and ask: 'What expectations did you carry into marriage that needed adjusting?' Let her honesty shape your own preparation.

insights.low: You may struggle to evaluate whether a partner is right for you, or you might choose based mainly on attraction or chemistry. Developing discernment prevents poor choices.
insights.medium: You consider some important factors when choosing a partner but might overlook red flags or become blind to certain incompatibilities.
insights.high: You evaluate partners thoughtfully, balancing attraction with values, character, and compatibility. This wise discernment leads to healthier relationships.
insights.microStep: Create a list of non-negotiable qualities in a partner — not just nice-to-haves, but dealbreakers for you.

genderLow.male: Men often choose partners based heavily on physical attraction or how a woman makes them feel. But chemistry fades — character, values, and emotional health are what sustain a marriage for decades.
genderLow.female: Women sometimes choose partners based on potential — 'who he could be' rather than who he actually is today. Marrying potential is one of the most common mistakes women make. Choose based on evidence, not hope.

genderMedium.male: You consider important factors, but you may overlook emotional health or spiritual maturity when attraction is strong. The wisest men evaluate character before chemistry.
genderMedium.female: You're thoughtful in evaluation, but you may rationalize red flags when you're emotionally invested. Trust your gut — if something feels off, it probably is. Don't talk yourself into someone.

genderHigh.male: A man who chooses a wife based on character, faith, and emotional health — not just attraction — protects his future family at the most fundamental level. Your discernment is wisdom in action.
genderHigh.female: A woman who evaluates partners with both her heart and her mind makes choices she won't have to survive later. Your discernment is one of your greatest protections.

genderMicroStep.male: Write down what you're primarily drawn to in a woman. Then write what you actually need in a wife for 40 years. Compare the two lists — where they differ is where your discernment needs sharpening.
genderMicroStep.female: Think about the last person you were interested in. Were you drawn to who they are — or who you wanted them to become? Practice evaluating the person in front of you, not the project.

insights.low: Past relationships may still significantly influence you. Unprocessed hurt or patterns repeat into new relationships. Healing work strengthens your readiness.
insights.medium: You've learned from past relationships but some patterns may still surface. Continued reflection helps you move forward without repeating history.
insights.high: You've integrated lessons from past relationships without being defined by them. You bring wisdom rather than wounds into new relationships.
insights.microStep: Reflect on your last significant relationship: What patterns do you see? Which do you want to avoid? Which strengths do you want to keep?

genderLow.male: Men often move on from past relationships without processing them — jumping into the next one or burying the pain under busyness. But unprocessed heartbreak shows up as walls, trust issues, or emotional unavailability in marriage.
genderLow.female: Women sometimes carry past relationship pain as a filter for every new connection — either idealizing what was lost or guarding against being hurt again. Neither approach lets you see a new person clearly.

genderMedium.male: You've learned from past relationships, but you may still carry subtle defensiveness or comparison patterns. Notice when you're reacting to a past wound rather than the present moment.
genderMedium.female: You've processed much of your past, but echoes may still surface — especially in moments of vulnerability or conflict. Stay curious about your reactions rather than defensive.

genderHigh.male: A man who has integrated his past relationships — owning his failures, releasing bitterness, and extracting wisdom — enters marriage as a learner, not a victim. That posture changes everything.
genderHigh.female: A woman who carries wisdom instead of wounds from past relationships is free to love without fear. Your integration work is one of the healthiest things you've done for your future marriage.

genderMicroStep.male: Write down what you contributed to the end of your last relationship — not what they did, but your part. Owning your role without shame frees you from repeating it.
genderMicroStep.female: Identify one fear from a past relationship that you're carrying into the future. Name it, then ask: 'Is this based on who I'm becoming, or who someone else was?'

insights.low: Juggling responsibilities is difficult for you. Marriage adds complexity — balancing work, home, relationship, and personal needs requires intentional prioritization.
insights.medium: You manage most things reasonably well but might struggle when competing demands arise. Developing systems helps prevent overwhelm in marriage.
insights.high: You prioritize what matters most and make intentional choices about how you spend time and energy. This discipline creates a healthy marriage.
insights.microStep: This week, identify your top 3 priorities. Spend 30 minutes on each. Notice how intentionality changes your week.

genderLow.male: Men who can't prioritize often hide behind busyness — confusing activity with purpose. Marriage doesn't need a man who does everything. It needs one who does the right things, on purpose.
genderLow.female: Women who struggle with priorities often say yes to everything and feel guilty about saying no. In marriage, this pattern leads to burnout and resentment. Learning to prioritize is an act of love — for yourself and your future spouse.

genderMedium.male: You manage most things, but you may default to work or personal goals when marriage demands shift your focus. Flexibility in priorities — without losing yourself — is a skill marriage requires.
genderMedium.female: You're reasonably organized, but competing demands may cause you to neglect your own needs. In marriage, a depleted wife can't sustain a healthy partnership. Your needs matter too.

genderHigh.male: A man who prioritizes intentionally — time with God, investment in relationships, purposeful work — creates a life his wife can trust and build alongside. Your discipline is a quiet form of leadership.
genderHigh.female: A woman who manages her priorities well brings order and intentionality to a marriage. Your ability to balance what matters without losing yourself is a rare and valuable strength.

genderMicroStep.male: Block 30 minutes this week for something that matters but isn't urgent — prayer, rest, a meaningful conversation. Notice how intentionality shifts your week.
genderMicroStep.female: This week, identify one thing you're doing out of obligation that drains you. Practice saying no to it — or delegating it. Reclaim that time for something life-giving.

insights.low: You may not see how your behavior affects others or understand your relational patterns. Self-awareness is the foundation for changing unhealthy dynamics.
insights.medium: You have some insight into how you relate but blind spots remain. Continuing to reflect on your impact strengthens relationships.
insights.high: You understand your relational patterns, triggers, and tendencies. This self-knowledge allows you to communicate and connect authentically.
insights.microStep: Ask someone you trust: 'When we're together, how do I make you feel?' Listen without defending. Notice patterns.

genderLow.male: Many men lack relational self-awareness because no one ever asked them to develop it. You may not realize how your silence, intensity, or distraction affects the people closest to you. That blind spot will cost you in marriage.
genderLow.female: Women are often more relationally aware of others than of themselves. You may read everyone else's emotions perfectly while ignoring your own patterns of control, withdrawal, or people-pleasing.

genderMedium.male: You have some awareness of how you come across, but feedback may still surprise you. The gap between how you see yourself and how others experience you is where your growth edge lives.
genderMedium.female: You know yourself fairly well, but relational blind spots tend to surface under stress. Pay attention to the patterns that appear when you're tired, anxious, or feeling unappreciated.

genderHigh.male: A man who understands his relational impact — who knows how his words, silence, and presence affect others — is a man people trust deeply. Your self-awareness makes you a safe partner.
genderHigh.female: A woman who knows her patterns, owns her triggers, and communicates with honesty brings clarity and depth to every relationship. Your self-awareness is a foundation your marriage will rest on.

genderMicroStep.male: Ask a close friend or family member: 'What's it like to be in relationship with me when I'm stressed?' Listen without defending. Write down what they say.
genderMicroStep.female: This week, notice one moment where you adjusted your behavior to manage someone else's emotions. Ask yourself: 'Was that wisdom, or was that people-pleasing?'

insights.low: You may prioritize your comfort over your partner's needs. Marriage requires flexibility and genuine sacrifice. Cultivating this willingness prepares you.
insights.medium: You're willing to sacrifice sometimes but might struggle when it costs you significantly. Growth here deepens your capacity for love.
insights.high: You understand sacrifice as an act of love, not burden. Your willingness to give generously creates a marriage where both people feel valued and cherished.
insights.microStep: Make one sacrifice this week — choose something your partner wants over what you want. Notice how it affects your connection.

genderLow.male: Men who struggle with sacrifice often frame it as independence. But marriage requires laying down preferences, time, and comfort regularly. A man who can't sacrifice remains a bachelor even after the wedding.
genderLow.female: Women who struggle with sacrifice may either give too much (losing themselves) or protect too fiercely (blocking intimacy). Healthy sacrifice is choosing your partner's good without abandoning your own needs.

genderMedium.male: You're willing to sacrifice when it's convenient — but marriage will ask you to sacrifice when it costs something real. Your financial comfort, your free time, your way of doing things. Growth here deepens love.
genderMedium.female: You sacrifice, but you may keep an internal scorecard. In marriage, score-keeping poisons generosity. Practice giving without tracking what you're owed in return.

genderHigh.male: A man who sacrifices joyfully — not out of duty but out of love — mirrors Christ's example. Your willingness to put your wife's needs alongside your own is the backbone of a thriving marriage.
genderHigh.female: A woman who can sacrifice without losing herself models a love that is both generous and wise. Your ability to give while maintaining your own identity creates a healthy, sustainable partnership.

genderMicroStep.male: This week, give up something you enjoy for the benefit of someone else — without mentioning it or expecting recognition. Notice what happens inside you.
genderMicroStep.female: This week, do something generous for someone — and then check your internal response. Are you expecting something back? Practice releasing the expectation.

insights.low: Your spiritual life may be inconsistent or passive. Faith difference or lack of shared spiritual foundation creates significant marital stress.
insights.medium: You have a spiritual foundation but it fluctuates. Building consistency creates a strong anchor for your marriage through all seasons.
insights.high: Your faith is consistent and integrated into how you live. A shared spiritual foundation provides guidance, hope, and resilience in marriage.
insights.microStep: Commit to one spiritual practice this week — prayer, Scripture, meditation, or service. Notice how it centers you.

genderLow.male: A man with an inconsistent spiritual life often drifts into leading from ego rather than faith. Without a grounded walk with God, you'll rely on your own strength — and marriage will expose its limits quickly.
genderLow.female: A woman with an inconsistent spiritual life may look to a husband to be her spiritual anchor — but that's a weight no man should carry alone. Your faith needs to stand on its own before it can intertwine with someone else's.

genderMedium.male: You have a real faith, but it may fluctuate with seasons or circumstances. A wife needs a man whose spiritual rhythm is steady — not perfect, but consistent. Build the habits now.
genderMedium.female: You have genuine faith, but it may ebb and flow with life's demands. Consistency in your walk with God will give you a foundation that doesn't shift when marriage gets hard.

genderHigh.male: A man whose faith is woven into his daily life creates a home where God's presence is felt, not just discussed. Your consistency here is spiritual leadership in its truest form.
genderHigh.female: A woman whose faith is integrated into her daily life brings spiritual depth and resilience to her marriage. Your consistency creates a home where both partners can grow closer to God.

genderMicroStep.male: Choose one spiritual discipline — prayer, Scripture reading, or fasting — and commit to it daily for the next 7 days. Don't aim for perfection. Aim for presence.
genderMicroStep.female: This week, set aside 15 minutes daily for intentional time with God — not rushed, not multitasked. Notice how it changes your emotional and relational temperature.

insights.low: Your understanding of spiritual leadership may be limited or unclear. Whether leading or following spiritually, clarity prevents conflict and confusion.
insights.medium: You have a basic understanding but haven't deeply thought through roles. Discussing this with a partner prevents misalignment.
insights.high: You understand spiritual leadership as mutual growth and service, not power or control. This maturity creates a healthy spiritual partnership.
insights.microStep: Reflect on what spiritual leadership means to you. How have you seen it modeled well? Poorly? What do you want in marriage?

genderLow.male: If spiritual leadership means authority without servanthood to you, your understanding needs rebuilding. Biblical leadership looks like washing feet, not giving orders. Your future wife needs a servant-leader, not a boss.
genderLow.female: If spiritual leadership is confusing or threatening to you, it may be because you've seen it done poorly. Healthy spiritual partnership is mutual growth and shared surrender to God — not hierarchy or control.

genderMedium.male: You have a foundation, but you may still be figuring out what spiritual leadership looks like practically. It's less about having all the answers and more about being the first to pray, repent, and pursue God together.
genderMedium.female: You understand the basics, but you may not have thought through what you actually want spiritual partnership to look like in your marriage. Clarity here prevents future frustration and misalignment.

genderHigh.male: A man who understands spiritual leadership as humble service, mutual submission, and shared faith creates a marriage where both partners flourish. This vision will attract a woman who values depth over control.
genderHigh.female: A woman who understands spiritual partnership — supporting, challenging, and growing alongside her husband in faith — brings a richness to marriage that transforms both people. Your clarity is a gift.

genderMicroStep.male: Ask yourself: 'If I were married today, how would I lead my wife spiritually — practically, not theoretically?' If you can't answer clearly, start studying what servant leadership looks like.
genderMicroStep.female: Write down what spiritual partnership means to you — not what someone told you it should mean, but what you actually want in a marriage. Use that as a filter for evaluating potential partners.

insights.low: Certain situations easily trigger strong reactions. Understanding your triggers helps you respond wisely rather than react defensively.
insights.medium: You're aware of some triggers but might be caught off-guard occasionally. Growing in trigger awareness prevents unnecessary conflict.
insights.high: You recognize your triggers and can pause before reacting. You communicate your needs clearly. This skill transforms potential conflict into connection.
insights.microStep: Identify 3 situations that reliably trigger strong emotions in you. What's the underlying fear or need beneath each trigger?

genderLow.male: Men's triggers often show up as anger, defensiveness, or control. That quick flash of rage or the urge to dominate a conversation? That's a trigger running the show. In marriage, unmanaged triggers become your wife's daily reality.
genderLow.female: Women's triggers often show up as anxiety, emotional shutdown, or the need to fix everything immediately. That overwhelming urgency you feel in certain moments? That's a trigger, not truth. Learning to pause changes everything.

genderMedium.male: You recognize some triggers, but recognition is just the start. The gap between knowing your trigger and changing your response is where the real work happens. Practice is everything.
genderMedium.female: You're aware of some triggers, but they may still catch you off-guard in intimate relationships. The closer someone is to you, the more power their actions have to activate old wounds. Prepare for that.

genderHigh.male: A man who knows his triggers and can pause before reacting creates safety in every room he enters. Your self-mastery in this area is one of the most protective gifts you'll bring to marriage.
genderHigh.female: A woman who understands her triggers and communicates her needs clearly transforms potential conflict into deeper understanding. Your self-awareness here is a rare and powerful strength.

genderMicroStep.male: Identify your top trigger. When it fires this week, commit to a 10-second pause: breathe, name the emotion, then choose your response deliberately instead of reacting.
genderMicroStep.female: Identify your top trigger and write down what you usually do when it activates. Then write down what you want to do instead. Keep that new response visible as a daily reminder.

insights.low: You carry unresolved wounds from your past. These often surface in relationships. Healing work before marriage prevents past hurt from damaging future love.
insights.medium: You've worked on healing but some wounds remain active. Continuing this work strengthens your capacity for healthy love and trust.
insights.high: You've processed past hurt and integrated those experiences wisely. You bring healing energy to your relationships rather than unresolved pain.
insights.microStep: Identify one past hurt that still affects you. Consider talking to a counselor, trusted friend, or spiritual mentor about it this month.

genderLow.male: Men often carry deep wounds beneath layers of toughness, humor, or detachment. The pain you haven't grieved doesn't disappear — it drives your behavior in hidden ways. Behind every controlling, angry, or emotionally distant husband is often an unhealed wound.
genderLow.female: Women often carry wounds that manifest as hyper-independence, anxiety, or an inability to trust. The hurt you haven't processed shapes who you let in and how close you let them get. Healing isn't optional — it's the path to real love.

genderMedium.male: You've done some healing work, but there may be wounds you've rationalized rather than resolved. If you notice recurring patterns — distrust, anger, withdrawal — there's likely something underneath that still needs attention.
genderMedium.female: You've made progress, but some wounds may still quietly influence your choices — who you're attracted to, what you tolerate, how quickly you trust. Stay in the process. Healing is ongoing, not a one-time event.

genderHigh.male: A man who has faced his wounds and done the hard work of healing brings strength and tenderness to his marriage. Your willingness to be honest about your pain makes you safe for someone else's vulnerability.
genderHigh.female: A woman who has walked through her pain and come out whole brings depth and compassion to every relationship. Your healing journey isn't just about you — it's a gift to the man who will one day receive your heart.

genderMicroStep.male: Name one wound you've been avoiding. Write it down simply: 'I was hurt by ___ when ___.' Consider sharing it with a counselor, pastor, or trusted mentor this month.
genderMicroStep.female: Identify one hurt that still stings when you think about it. Ask yourself: 'Have I truly processed this, or have I just learned to function around it?' Take one step toward genuine healing this month.

questions.text: You just received deeply disappointing news. Within the next hour, you need to show up for a friend who needs you. What happens inside you?

options.text: I feel it, name it, and set it aside. I can return to it when I have space

genderInsight.male: Your emotional steadiness is a real asset. In a culture that often tells men to shut down feeling, your ability to feel AND stay grounded is strength, not softness.
genderInsight.female: Your emotional steadiness gives you the capacity to hold space for both yourself and a future partner. This is a foundation others will lean on.

options.text: I tell my friend I am going through something too, but I am here for them. I process by sharing

genderInsight.male: Reaching out to process is healthy — and rarer in men than you might think. Sharing your struggle while showing up for someone else is a sign of relational maturity, not weakness.
genderInsight.female: Processing through connection is natural and healthy. Just make sure you're also building the ability to sit with hard feelings independently when you need to — marriage will ask for both.

options.text: I push it down and show up, but I would probably seem distracted or off

genderInsight.male: This pattern is common in men and often invisible because culture rewards 'toughness.' But in marriage, this pattern creates distance and confusion for your partner.
genderInsight.female: This pattern may be protecting you now, but in marriage it will create a gap between what you feel and what your partner experiences. That gap becomes loneliness.

options.text: I would struggle to be present. The disappointment would consume me and I might cancel

genderInsight.male: Getting consumed by disappointment to the point where you can't show up for others is a pattern worth watching. In marriage, your wife will need you present even on your worst days.
genderInsight.female: When disappointment takes over, it signals your emotional reserves are low. In marriage, hard days don't pause for your feelings — building capacity to be present through pain is essential.

phase.title: Who You Are
phase.description: Let's start with how you're wired emotionally and spiritually.

genderVariant.male: You just received deeply disappointing news. Within the next hour, you need to show up for a friend who needs your support. What happens inside you?
genderVariant.female: You just received deeply disappointing news. Within the next hour, you need to be present for a friend who needs your support. What happens inside you?

questions.text: You have been dating someone for a few months. They have not replied in two days, unusual for them. What is your first thought?

options.text: They are probably busy or going through something. I will check in when it feels right, not spiral over it

genderInsight.male: Secure attachment in men often looks like steady presence without possessiveness — you can hold space for a partner without needing to control the outcome.
genderInsight.female: Your secure attachment means you can be fully invested without being consumed. This groundedness will attract and sustain a healthy partnership.

options.text: I hope I did not do something wrong. I replay our last conversation in my head looking for clues

genderInsight.male: Insecure attachment in men often hides behind independence or intensity. Recognizing your pattern is the first step to changing it.
genderInsight.female: Your attachment pattern shapes how you love, fight, and connect. Understanding it gives you power to choose differently.

options.text: If they wanted to talk to me, they would. I am not chasing anyone. I pull back too

genderInsight.male: Insecure attachment in men often hides behind independence or intensity. Recognizing your pattern is the first step to changing it.
genderInsight.female: Your attachment pattern shapes how you love, fight, and connect. Understanding it gives you power to choose differently.

options.text: I feel unsettled but would rather wait than risk looking needy, even though the silence is eating at me

genderInsight.male: You're aware of your patterns and growing. That awareness is itself a sign of health — it means you can choose differently when the old wiring activates.
genderInsight.female: You're aware of your patterns, which is half the battle. Keep building the muscle of choosing presence over protection.

questions.text:
Someone you trust says: "When we talk, I feel like you are not really listening, like you are just waiting for your turn to speak."
What is your honest first reaction?

options.text: That would sting, but I would want to hear more. If that is their experience, I need to understand it

genderInsight.male: Receiving hard feedback without defensiveness is a leadership quality that will define your marriage. Many men hear criticism and fight back — your openness makes you safe to be honest with.
genderInsight.female: Your willingness to sit with uncomfortable feedback shows emotional security. In marriage, your husband will need to be able to tell you hard truths — this openness invites that.

options.text: I would feel defensive at first, but after sitting with it, I would probably see some truth in it

genderInsight.male: The defensive-then-reflective pattern is common in men and actually workable — as long as you eventually come back and own it. The gap between reaction and reflection is where growth happens.
genderInsight.female: Initial defensiveness followed by genuine reflection shows you're still processing, not shutting down. The key is shortening the gap between the flinch and the honest response.

options.text: I would feel hurt and misunderstood. I would probably explain why I do that rather than receive it

genderInsight.male: Explaining instead of listening is a defensive pattern many men use — turning feedback into a debate rather than an opportunity to learn. Your future wife needs to know her observations will be received, not argued.
genderInsight.female: Responding to feedback by justifying your behavior protects your ego but blocks growth. In marriage, your husband's perspective on your patterns is valuable data — even when it stings.

options.text: Something in me shuts down. Feedback like that makes me question whether the relationship is safe, even if my reaction is bigger than the moment

genderInsight.male: Shutting down under feedback means criticism feels like an existential threat. For men, this often connects to a core belief that being wrong means being inadequate. Marriage will surface this constantly.
genderInsight.female: If feedback makes you question the whole relationship, you may be connecting criticism to your worth. In marriage, your husband needs to be able to name concerns without you disappearing.

questions.text: Think about the hardest season you have been through: a loss, a failure, deep stress. How did you come through it?

options.text: Faith, community, and healthy habits carried me through. Not perfectly, but I came out more grounded

genderInsight.male: Leaning into faith, community, and healthy habits during crisis is rare in men, who are socialized to handle things alone. This resilience pattern will anchor a future home.
genderInsight.female: Your ability to draw on multiple support systems during crisis shows real strength. Many women shoulder hardship in isolation while appearing fine — your pattern of seeking help is wiser.

options.text: I survived it, but I mostly pushed through on my own. It took a lot out of me
options.outcomeLabel: endures alone, rarely asks for help

genderInsight.male: Pushing through alone is the default male script for hard seasons. It works — until marriage, where your wife will feel shut out of your pain and wonder why you won't let her in.
genderInsight.female: Independent endurance feels strong but it's lonely. In marriage, going it alone during hard seasons creates distance — your husband will want to carry weight with you.

options.text: Distraction, overworking, or numbing got me through it. Functional on the outside, unprocessed on the inside

genderInsight.male: Distraction and numbing are the most common male coping strategies — work, screens, substances, staying busy. They get you through the crisis but leave you hollow. Marriage needs a man who processes, not one who hides.
genderInsight.female: Overworking or numbing to survive hard seasons is understandable but leaves the pain unprocessed. In marriage, coping patterns that avoid feeling become patterns that avoid intimacy.

options.text: It broke me. Hard seasons still scare me because the last one showed me how little I can hold on my own

genderInsight.male: Falling apart under pressure isn't weakness — but it signals you haven't yet built the coping foundation marriage demands. Men who don't develop resilience before marriage often crumble within it.
genderInsight.female: Hard seasons that overwhelm you completely suggest your internal resources need building. Marriage will bring plenty of hard seasons — developing resilience now protects your future family.

questions.text: If someone looked at your last 90 days, not your intentions but your actual life, how much evidence of active faith would they find?

options.text: Real evidence. Not perfect consistency, but someone watching my life would see faith in my choices, my community, and my time

genderInsight.male: A man with visible, consistent faith creates spiritual safety in a home. This isn't about perfection — it's about rhythm and authenticity.
genderInsight.female: Your consistent faith practice shows that your spiritual life is integrated, not compartmentalized. This will anchor a future marriage.

options.text: Some evidence in seasons. I go through strong weeks and quiet ones, but faith is real to me

genderInsight.male: Growth in spiritual consistency is normal. For men especially, faith often moves from head knowledge to lived practice over time.
genderInsight.female: Your faith is real but still finding its rhythm. Consistency isn't perfection — it's showing up even when you don't feel like it.

options.text: Not much. I believe but I do not practice consistently enough for it to show

genderInsight.male: Low spiritual practice often reflects disconnection from community or unresolved doubt. Marriage without shared spiritual ground will feel lonely.
genderInsight.female: Private faith is still faith — but marriage thrives on shared spiritual life. Consider what's keeping your practice private.

options.text: More confusion than clarity. I am still figuring out what I believe and how it fits my life

genderInsight.male: Faith in question is not uncommon, and it's honest. But entering marriage without spiritual clarity means building on uncertain ground.
genderInsight.female: Questioning your faith takes courage. But the answers you find (or don't) will shape what kind of marriage you build.

questions.text: You catch yourself responding to someone you love the way a parent used to: a certain tone, a withdrawal, a controlling comment. What happens next?

options.text: I notice it and course-correct. I have done enough work on my family patterns to catch them in real time

genderInsight.male: Real-time pattern interruption means you've done the inner work most men avoid — actually examining your father's influence and choosing differently. This protects your future family.
genderInsight.female: Catching inherited patterns in the moment shows deep self-work. Many many women don't realize their mother's relational habits have been absorbed until they surface in marriage — your awareness is ahead of the curve.

options.text: I realize it afterward and feel convicted. I am learning to recognize the pattern even if I cannot always stop it in the moment
options.outcomeLabel: slow to catch it, but learning

genderInsight.male: Catching it after is still catching it. Many men never examine their father's patterns at all. The fact that you feel conviction means the awareness is building.
genderInsight.female: Recognizing the pattern afterward shows growing awareness. Each time you notice, the gap shortens. This kind of self-examination will serve your marriage well.

options.text: Someone else would probably notice before I do. I do not always see how my family patterns show up

genderInsight.male: Low pattern awareness means you're running your father's software without knowing it. A wife will see these patterns clearly — the question is whether you'll be open when she names them.
genderInsight.female: If others see your inherited patterns before you do, you're operating with blind spots that will surface in marriage. The habits you don't recognize are the ones you can't change.

options.text: I would not see the connection. I do not think about my parents' patterns much or how they affect me

genderInsight.male: Not seeing the connection between your family of origin and your current behavior is one of the most dangerous blind spots a man can bring into marriage. What you don't see, you repeat.
genderInsight.female: Unexamined family inheritance is how unhealthy patterns survive across generations. The behaviors you inherited from your parents will show up in your marriage — the only question is whether you'll see them coming.

questions.text: A close friend says something that offends you during a group conversation. They do not seem to realize it. What do you do?

options.text: I bring it up privately later. I want to understand what they meant before I assume the worst

genderInsight.male: Approaching conflict with curiosity rather than defensiveness is uncommon in men and incredibly valuable. Your future wife will feel safe bringing hard things to you.
genderInsight.female: Your conflict approach shows courage and relational skill. Being able to engage directly without attacking or withdrawing is a powerful foundation.

options.text: Grace first. Let it go in the moment and only address it if a pattern forms. One-offs do not need a conversation

genderInsight.male: You're learning to navigate tension — that's good. Many men default to either fighting or fleeing. Finding the middle ground takes practice.
genderInsight.female: You're growing in how you handle tension. The tendency to absorb conflict without addressing it is common for women — watch for that pattern.

options.text: Silence, but the kind that changes things. Something shifts in how I see them, even if they never know why

genderInsight.male: Withdrawal or avoidance in conflict is the most common male pattern — and Gottman's research shows it's one of the biggest predictors of relationship failure.
genderInsight.female: Whether you go silent or escalate, this pattern will define how safe your marriage feels. The good news: conflict skills can be learned.

options.text: I would probably respond in the moment. I find it hard to let things sit when I feel disrespected

genderInsight.male: Withdrawal or avoidance in conflict is the most common male pattern — and Gottman's research shows it's one of the biggest predictors of relationship failure.
genderInsight.female: Whether you go silent or escalate, this pattern will define how safe your marriage feels. The good news: conflict skills can be learned.

phase.title: How You Relate
phase.description: Now let's explore how you navigate relationships and conflict.

questions.text: Someone you care about says something that wounds you. They meant it as a joke, but it hit a nerve. What happens inside you first?

options.text: The sting lands, but my mouth stays steady. I express that it hurt me and explain why, without matching their aggressive energy

genderInsight.male: Being able to name your pain without attacking is the kind of emotional leadership that builds deep safety in a marriage.
genderInsight.female: Speaking hurt clearly without weaponizing it is a sign of remarkable emotional health. Your future spouse will feel safe being honest with you.

options.text: I go quiet, not because I am shutting down, but because I need to understand what I feel before I can speak

genderInsight.male: Being able to name your pain without attacking is the kind of emotional leadership that builds deep safety in a marriage.
genderInsight.female: Speaking hurt clearly without weaponizing it is a sign of remarkable emotional health. Your future spouse will feel safe being honest with you.

options.text: A laugh, a subject change, and a replay loop for three days, wishing I had said something in the moment

genderInsight.male: Hiding hurt while replaying it internally is exhausting. What you store privately will eventually leak into the relationship sideways.
genderInsight.female: The gap between what you show and what you feel erodes intimacy over time. Your future partner deserves to know what's really happening inside you.

options.text: I snap back with something sharp. When I feel hurt, my instinct is to hurt back or shut them out

genderInsight.male: Retaliation or shutdown when hurt is a protective reflex that destroys safety in marriage. This pattern is worth focused attention.
genderInsight.female: This reactive pattern protects you in the moment but costs you the relationship long-term. There's a middle ground between doormat and fortress.

genderVariant.male: Someone you care about says something that wounds you. They meant it as a joke but it cut deep, touching something real. Your first instinct is to:
genderVariant.female: Someone you care about says something that wounds you. They meant it as a joke but it cut deep, touching something you carry quietly. Your first instinct is to:

questions.text: You have been dating someone for several months. The chemistry is strong and they are kind to you, but they avoid hard conversations, rarely talk about faith, and their closest friends worry you. What do you do?

options.text: I bring it up directly. Chemistry is not enough if character and values are unclear

genderInsight.male: Character-driven evaluation over chemistry is powerful — and hard for men who are often led by physical attraction and how someone makes them feel. This discipline will protect you.
genderInsight.female: Your ability to evaluate character over connection is crucial. Many women are often told to follow their heart — but your head's involvement in partner selection will save your marriage before it starts.

options.text: I give it more time. People reveal themselves gradually, and I do not want to judge too early

genderInsight.male: Patience is good, but passivity is different. Men sometimes confuse 'giving it time' with avoiding the hard conversation. Don't let months pass hoping a concern resolves itself.
genderInsight.female: Waiting to see more is wise within reason. But watch for the pattern of hoping he changes rather than evaluating who he actually is. Long observation windows can become delayed decision-making.

options.text: I focus on how they treat me. The rest will work itself out if the love is real
options.outcomeLabel: led by feelings and overlook red flags

genderInsight.male: Focusing on how she treats you while ignoring broader character patterns is a dangerous shortcut. Marriage reveals everything — her friend circle, conflict style, and faith will shape your daily life.
genderInsight.female: Believing love will cover the gaps is a common hope that rarely survives marriage. How he treats YOU is important — but who he IS when you're not watching matters more long-term.

options.text: The chemistry would probably keep me in it longer than I should stay. I have a hard time walking away when I feel connected

genderInsight.male: If chemistry overrides your judgment, you're likely to marry based on attraction and discover incompatibility too late. Physical and emotional chemistry fades — character is what remains.
genderInsight.female: Staying too long because of chemistry is one of the most common patterns in women's dating stories. The pull you feel is real, but it's not a reliable signal of long-term compatibility.

questions.text: Someone you care about does something that makes you truly angry, not just annoyed. You feel the heat rising. What do you do in the next 60 seconds?

options.text: I feel it fully but I do not let it drive my next words or actions. I choose how to express it, not whether to
options.outcomeLabel: feels the anger, chooses the response

genderInsight.male: Feeling genuine anger without letting it choose your next words is the hardest emotional regulation test for men. Anger is faster and louder than other emotions — your ability to pause mid-surge protects everyone around you.
genderInsight.female: Choosing your response when anger is hot shows you've developed the space between feeling and action. In marriage, this means your husband can make you angry without fearing your reaction.

options.text: I remove myself. I know I need space before I can respond without saying something I will regret
options.outcomeLabel: steps away to protect the relationship

genderInsight.male: Your emotional steadiness is a real asset. In a culture that often tells men to shut down feeling, your ability to feel AND stay grounded is strength, not softness.
genderInsight.female: Your emotional steadiness gives you the capacity to hold space for both yourself and a future partner. This is a foundation others will lean on.

options.text: I go cold. My voice drops, I shut down emotionally, and I give very short answers until it passes

genderInsight.male: Going cold when angry — shutting down, giving one-word answers, withdrawing warmth — is a controlled form of punishment. It feels safer than exploding, but your future wife will experience your silence as emotional abandonment.
genderInsight.female: Cold shutdown in anger is often learned from environments where expressing anger wasn't safe. In marriage, your husband will feel the temperature drop and know something is wrong, but be locked out from resolving it.

options.text: The anger comes out: raised voice, sharp words, slamming something. I regret it later but in the moment I cannot stop it

genderInsight.male: This is worth taking seriously. Unmanaged emotional patterns in men often show up as anger, withdrawal, or shutdown — all of which damage closeness.
genderInsight.female: This is worth taking seriously. When emotions control your responses, it affects your ability to be present, safe, and consistent for a partner.

genderVariant.male: Someone you care about does something that makes you truly angry, not just annoyed. You feel the heat rising, your jaw tightening. What do you do in the next 60 seconds?
