genderVariant.female: Someone you care about does something that makes you truly angry, not just annoyed. You feel the heat rising, the words forming. What do you do in the next 60 seconds?

questions.text: Someone you trusted shared private information about you with others. When you think about it a month later, what is most true?

options.text: Forgiven and adjusted. The relationship survived, but what I share with them has changed. Wisdom and forgiveness coexist

genderInsight.male: Forgiveness with healthy boundaries is the gold standard. Many men either forgive and pretend nothing happened, or cut people off entirely. Your middle path shows real maturity.
genderInsight.female: Forgiving while adjusting trust is sophisticated emotional work. Many women forgive and then reopen the same level of access — your wisdom to readjust shows relational intelligence.

options.text: I have moved past the anger but I still feel guarded around them. The trust has shifted
options.outcomeLabel: past the anger but still guarded

genderInsight.male: Moving past anger while remaining guarded is honest. The question for men is: will you ever address this directly, or will you just slowly fade the friendship without explaining why?
genderInsight.female: Residual guardedness after betrayal is normal. The growth edge for you is whether you can name this shift to the person — 'I'm still working through what happened' — rather than just quietly pulling back.

options.text: I say I forgive you, but emotionally something still stirs when I think about it

genderInsight.male: Saying forgiveness while still carrying the charge means the forgiveness is incomplete. Men often declare forgiveness as a decision but skip the emotional release. Your body knows the difference.
genderInsight.female: Verbal forgiveness with lingering resentment is honest but unsustainable. In marriage, unforgiveness leaks into everything — tone, trust, and how safe your husband feels to fail.

options.text: I cannot pretend to be fine with what they did. Trust like that does not come back easily for me
options.outcomeLabel: honest about pain, stuck in unforgiveness

genderInsight.male: Honest pain held without movement toward forgiveness becomes bitterness over time. Marriage will wound you deeper than any friendship — if you can't forgive a friend, you're not yet equipped for a spouse.
genderInsight.female: Holding pain honestly shows integrity, but staying stuck in it limits your capacity for intimacy. If trust can't be rebuilt after breach, every relationship has an expiration date.

questions.text: A married couple you respect disagree about a major decision. One feels God leading one way; the other feels differently. They ask your perspective. What do you say?

options.text: Pray together, seek counsel, and wait for unity. God does not usually lead a couple in two different directions at the same time

genderInsight.male: Mutual discernment honors both voices. As a man, this means your future leadership is measured by how well you listen, not how decisively you decide.
genderInsight.female: Valuing mutual discernment means your future marriage won't have a silenced partner. This posture protects your voice and invites genuine partnership.

options.text: I would ask who usually takes the lead spiritually and encourage that person to seek God more deeply. Someone needs to lead

genderInsight.male: Structured headship carries weight — it means your leadership is judged by how well your wife flourishes under it, not by how often you get the final word. Servant leadership, not authority.
genderInsight.female: If you lean toward structured headship, make sure your understanding of it is biblical, not cultural. Headship means your husband sacrifices like Christ — not that you silence yourself.

options.text: I would tell them to follow their individual convictions. God speaks to each person personally

genderInsight.male: Individual spiritual autonomy sounds freeing but creates a marriage with no shared spiritual ground. A home needs a shared direction — even if each person walks it differently.
genderInsight.female: Each following their own leading works in friendships but creates spiritual loneliness in marriage. Consider what it means to build a home with someone whose faith life never intersects yours.

options.text: I would not know what to say. Spiritual leadership in marriage is not something I have thought through yet

genderInsight.male: Not having a theology of spiritual partnership before marriage is like building without blueprints. Your wife will need to know how you approach shared spiritual decisions.
genderInsight.female: Without clarity here, you're vulnerable to accepting someone else's framework by default. Do the theological work now so you choose a partner who matches your conviction, not one who defines it for you.

genderVariant.male: A married couple you respect disagree about a major decision. One feels God leading one way; the other feels differently. As a man thinking about leading a home, which approach feels right to you?
genderVariant.female: A married couple you respect disagree about a major decision. One feels God leading one way; the other feels differently. As a woman thinking about what spiritual partnership should look like, which approach feels right to you?

questions.text: Someone you are dating unintentionally touches on something from your childhood that still carries pain: an absent parent, a broken home, a deep rejection. What happens inside you?

options.text: The tenderness is there, and I can acknowledge it as a sensitive area without falling apart or leaving the conversation
options.outcomeLabel: can share openly without being destabilized

genderInsight.male: Being able to share childhood pain with a dating partner without being thrown off shows rare emotional capacity in a man. Your future wife will feel safe knowing you can be vulnerable without breaking.
genderInsight.female: Openness about past wounds without being overwhelmed shows you've processed them well. This capacity for vulnerable strength will create deep safety in your marriage.

options.text: I feel a wave of emotion but I manage it. I might change the subject and come back to it when I feel safe enough

genderInsight.male: Managing the wave and coming back to it later is a healthy strategy. The key for men is actually coming back — many men feel the emotion, manage it, and then never revisit it.
genderInsight.female: Feeling the wave and managing it shows both sensitivity and strength. Make sure 'coming back when ready' actually happens rather than becoming permanent avoidance.

options.text: I shut down or deflect. I do not want them to see that part of me yet, maybe ever

genderInsight.male: Shutting down when vulnerable topics arise is one of the most common ways men protect themselves — but in marriage, your wife will feel locked out of the most important parts of you.
genderInsight.female: Deflecting vulnerability protects you in the moment but creates emotional distance. The parts of yourself you hide are often the parts your future husband most needs to know.

options.text: It hits me hard. I might tear up, get angry, or emotionally flood in a way that surprises even me

genderInsight.male: Emotional flooding when wounds are touched means the pain is still raw and active. A man who floods in vulnerable moments often switches to anger or shutdown — both of which damage trust.
genderInsight.female: Flooding when old wounds are touched means they haven't been adequately processed. In marriage, your husband will inevitably touch these places — building capacity to hold the pain is essential.

phase.title: What You Carry
phase.description: This section goes deeper — into the wounds, patterns, and triggers you bring into relationships.

questions.text: You start dating someone new and they do something that reminds you of a painful pattern from a past relationship. What do you notice happening in yourself?

options.text: I notice the similarity but I can separate the two people. I evaluate this person on their own merits, not my past

genderInsight.male: Separating past from present requires real emotional discipline. Men who can evaluate a new partner on her own terms — without projecting old hurts — build healthier relationships.
genderInsight.female: Seeing each person clearly, without layering past experiences on top of them, is rare and valuable. Your future husband deserves to be known for who he is, not feared for what someone else did.

options.text: It triggers a warning in me. I am aware it might be my past talking, but I watch more carefully from that point

genderInsight.male: Awareness that your past might be coloring your perception is itself a strength. Many many men don't recognize when they're reacting to a ghost rather than the person in front of them.
genderInsight.female: Heightened alertness from past pain is your nervous system trying to protect you. The growth edge is distinguishing between actual red flags and trauma-activated false alarms.

options.text: I pull back emotionally. I do not want to say it is because of my past, but something shifts inside me

genderInsight.male: Pulling back without knowing why means your past is driving your present without your awareness. In marriage, this shows up as unexplained distance that leaves your wife confused and hurt.
genderInsight.female: Emotional withdrawal you can't explain to yourself or your partner is your nervous system making decisions for you. Understanding the trigger gives you back the choice.

options.text: A strong urge to end it because I sense I have been here before, and my past decides before my mind catches up

genderInsight.male: If past pain makes you want to run at the first sign of a familiar pattern, your past is choosing your future. Marriage to a real person requires seeing them — not seeing through them to someone else.
genderInsight.female: Refusing to go through pain again is understandable but limiting. If many a man who reminds you of a past wound gets eliminated, you'll either be alone or choose someone who triggers nothing — which usually means no depth.

questions.text: Someone close to you raises their voice during a disagreement. Not yelling, but their tone shifts sharply. Something in you reacts before you can think. What happens?

options.text: I notice it in my body—chest tightens, jaw clenches—but I can pause and ask for a moment before I respond
options.outcomeLabel: feels it in the body but pauses

genderInsight.male: Feeling the somatic trigger and pausing before reacting is advanced emotional regulation. For men, whose anger response can be fast and physical, this pause is the difference between safety and damage.
genderInsight.female: Noticing your body's alarm while choosing your response is powerful self-regulation. This means your future husband can have hard conversations with you without walking on eggshells.

options.text: Imperfect but present. The trigger fires, my body tenses, but I stay in the conversation even if I do not handle it perfectly

genderInsight.male: Staying in it imperfectly is still staying in it. Many men leave the conversation — physically or emotionally — the moment tension rises. Your willingness to stay, even poorly, is a foundation to build on.
genderInsight.female: Imperfect presence is still presence. The fact that you stay in the conversation when triggered shows courage — and each time you do it, the trigger loses a little power.

options.text: Silence takes over. Something in me shuts down and words disappear, even when I want to speak

genderInsight.male: The freeze response — going silent when tension rises — often comes from childhood experiences where speaking up was unsafe. In marriage, your silence will feel like punishment to your wife even when you don't intend it.
genderInsight.female: Shutting down when voices rise is often a learned survival response. In marriage, your silence in conflict will leave your husband guessing what's wrong and unable to reach you.

options.text: I match their energy or escalate. If they come at me with heat, I fire back before I can stop myself

genderInsight.male: Matching energy or escalating is an aggressive pattern that makes you unsafe to disagree with. A wife who can't raise a concern without you firing back will stop being honest — and the marriage will suffocate.
genderInsight.female: Escalation in response to tension creates an environment where no one can bring up problems safely. In marriage, this pattern ensures small issues become big ones because nothing gets addressed early.

questions.text: A relationship is going well. This person is kind, consistent, and clearly into you. You start to feel yourself falling for them. What happens next inside you?

options.text: I let myself enjoy it. I can receive love without needing to control the outcome or protect myself from it

genderInsight.male: Being able to receive love without needing to control it or protect against it is uncommon in men. When closeness feels safe rather than threatening, you'll build deep intimacy rather than managed distance.
genderInsight.female: Letting yourself fall without bracing for the crash shows your attachment system trusts the process. In marriage, this openness allows intimacy to deepen rather than plateauing at 'safe.'

options.text: Excitement mixed with caution, as part of me starts looking for reasons it might not work

genderInsight.male: You're aware of your patterns and growing. That awareness is itself a sign of health — it means you can choose differently when the old wiring activates.
genderInsight.female: You're aware of your patterns, which is half the battle. Keep building the muscle of choosing presence over protection.

options.text: I pull back slightly. Something about being truly wanted makes me uncomfortable, even though I want it

genderInsight.male: Pulling back when someone gets close is the avoidant pattern in action — and it's more common in men than most realize. You want connection but the closeness itself triggers an exit impulse. Your future wife will feel this as rejection.
genderInsight.female: Discomfort with being wanted often traces back to early experiences where closeness led to pain. Recognizing this as a pattern — not a preference — is the first step toward changing it.

options.text: The grip tightens: more checking in, more needing reassurance, more anxiety about losing them. Closeness and panic come together

genderInsight.male: Insecure attachment in men often hides behind independence or intensity. Recognizing your pattern is the first step to changing it.
genderInsight.female: Your attachment pattern shapes how you love, fight, and connect. Understanding it gives you power to choose differently.

questions.text: You and a close friend had a tense conversation two weeks ago. It was never fully resolved. Both of you moved on without addressing it. How do you carry that now?

options.text: It bothers me that it is unresolved. I would bring it up to clear the air, even if it is awkward

genderInsight.male: Going back to resolve lingering tension — even weeks later — shows relational courage. Many men let unresolved conversations die quietly and wonder why friendships and marriages slowly lose depth.
genderInsight.female: Pursuing resolution when it would be easier to let it go shows you value the relationship more than your comfort. In marriage, this instinct prevents the silent buildup that erodes trust over years.

options.text: I have mostly let it go but I notice a slight distance between us. I am not sure how to bring it back up
options.outcomeLabel: notices the distance but unsure how to bridge it

genderInsight.male: Noticing the distance without knowing how to bridge it is where most men get stuck. You sense the relational temperature but lack the script to address it. This is a learnable skill, not a character flaw.
genderInsight.female: Feeling the gap but being unsure how to close it is honest. The fact that you notice the emotional shift shows emotional awareness — what's missing is the confidence to act on what you sense.

options.text: I have filed it away, but if something similar happens, it will come back stronger because it was never resolved

genderInsight.male: Filing away unresolved tension and waiting for the next offense to cash it all in is a dangerous pattern. Men who store conflict rather than process it build invisible resentment that explodes more than the situation calls for.
genderInsight.female: Storing unresolved tension means every new friction carries the weight of old frictions. In marriage, this backlog turns small disagreements into 'you always' conversations.

options.text: I have already adjusted how much I trust or share with them. Unresolved conflict quietly changes my relationships

genderInsight.male: This conflict pattern will actively damage any close relationship. Consider working with a counselor specifically on conflict engagement.
genderInsight.female: This pattern will make it very hard for a partner to feel safe raising concerns. Conflict skills are learnable — this is worth investing in.

questions.text:
A newly married friend tells you: "Marriage is the best thing that ever happened to me. We never fight and I have never been happier."
What is your reaction?

options.text: I am happy for them but that is probably the honeymoon phase. Real marriage includes conflict and hard work alongside the joy

genderInsight.male: Seeing through the honeymoon narrative shows maturity. Many men enter marriage expecting it to fulfill them — your realistic expectations protect you from crushing disappointment.
genderInsight.female: Grounded expectations are a gift. Many women enter marriage with a 'happily ever after' script and feel something is wrong when reality doesn't match. Your realism protects the real thing.

options.text: That is exactly what I want: a marriage where we are so connected that conflict rarely happens

genderInsight.male: Wanting a conflict-free marriage is a fantasy that will leave you unprepared for reality. The strongest marriages include productive disagreement — men who avoid all conflict often avoid depth.
genderInsight.female: Idealizing a conflict-free marriage sets you up for disappointment when real disagreements arrive. Healthy marriages fight well — they don't avoid fighting.

options.text: I feel a mix of hope and skepticism. I want that, but part of me wonders if it is too good to be true

genderInsight.male: Healthy skepticism mixed with hope is an honest place to be. The key for men is not letting skepticism harden into cynicism — you can hope for great while preparing for hard.
genderInsight.female: Hope and skepticism in tension is honest. Let both voices speak — the hope keeps you open, the skepticism keeps you grounded.

options.text: I feel envious or discouraged. I wonder if I will ever have something like that

genderInsight.male: Envy or discouragement reveals that marriage has become a measuring stick for your life's value. No man enters a healthy marriage from a place of 'I need this to feel complete.'
genderInsight.female: Feeling left behind or not enough is painful — but entering marriage from envy leads to choosing out of desperation rather than discernment. Your completeness can't come from another person.

questions.text: You are strongly attracted to someone who does not share your faith, values, or vision for family, but the connection feels electric. They want to take things further. What do you do?

options.text: I have clear boundaries for this. No matter how strong the pull, I am not willing to build a future on a foundation I know is unstable

genderInsight.male: Holding conviction over chemistry is especially hard for men, where physical attraction can override logic. Your boundary here protects your future family from being built on sand.
genderInsight.female: Clear values boundaries in dating protects you from the pattern many women fall into — believing love can change someone's fundamental orientation. It can't.

options.text: I would slow things down and test whether the values gap is real or surface-level, but I would not let chemistry drive the decision

genderInsight.male: Testing whether the gap is real shows wisdom. Just set a clear timeline — men can 'evaluate' indefinitely while emotional attachment deepens, making the eventual decision harder.
genderInsight.female: Cautious evaluation is wise, but watch for the subtle slide from 'testing' to 'hoping they'll change.' Give it a real timeline and honest criteria.

options.text: I would struggle. I know what I should do but the connection might pull me in before I make a clear-headed choice

genderInsight.male: Desire competing with conviction is an honest battle. For men, physical attraction is often the strongest pull — knowing this about yourself gives you power to choose wisely even when your body disagrees.
genderInsight.female: Knowing what you should do while feeling pulled toward what you want is human. The question is which voice wins when it matters. Building that muscle now determines your future choices.

options.text: I would probably go with it. Life is short and maybe love is enough even without shared values
options.outcomeLabel: lives in the moment, avoids planning

genderInsight.male: Living for now in matters of the heart means your future marriage will be built on chemistry that fades. The passion you feel today cannot sustain a 50-year covenant.
genderInsight.female: Believing love is enough without shared values is romantic but dangerous. Marriage amplifies differences — what feels exciting now becomes a daily source of friction later.

phase.title: Where You're Going
phase.description: Finally, let's look at your expectations and readiness for what's ahead.

questions.text: Your spouse (or future spouse) receives a dream opportunity that requires significant sacrifice from you: changing your plans, giving up something important, or relocating somewhere you do not want to go. What is your honest reaction?

options.text: I would immediately support them. Their happiness matters more to me than my own preferences
options.outcomeLabel: gives too quickly, may lose themselves

genderInsight.male: Counting the cost is wise. Marriage will ask real things of you — knowing your limits protects both you and your partner.
genderInsight.female: Your awareness of the cost of sacrifice is healthy. Women who don't count the cost often end up depleted.

options.text: The tension would be real and it would cost me, but working through it together is what love looks like
options.outcomeLabel: feels the cost but chooses love

genderInsight.male: Feeling the cost and choosing love anyway — this is mature sacrifice. It's not about being the hero; it's about being honest and still showing up.
genderInsight.female: Eyes-open sacrifice is the healthiest kind. You can count the cost without being controlled by it.

options.text: I would need to weigh how much this costs me. I want to be supportive but I also need my life to work for me

genderInsight.male: Counting the cost is wise. Marriage will ask real things of you — knowing your limits protects both you and your partner.
genderInsight.female: Your awareness of the cost of sacrifice is healthy. Women who don't count the cost often end up depleted.

options.text: Deep resistance. Giving up major things for someone else's dream does not feel like love; it feels like loss

genderInsight.male: Marriage requires genuine sacrifice. If giving up something important for love feels impossible, that's important information about your readiness.
genderInsight.female: Marriage without sacrifice is just cohabitation. If this feels impossible right now, explore what's driving the resistance.

genderVariant.male: Your wife (or future wife) receives a dream opportunity that requires significant sacrifice from you: relocating away from your career, your community, or your comfort zone. What is your honest response?
genderVariant.female: Your husband (or future husband) receives a dream opportunity that requires significant sacrifice from you: putting your goals on hold, leaving your community, or adjusting your life around his. What is your honest response?

questions.text: Think about the deepest emotional wound you carry: from family, a relationship, a betrayal, or a loss. What have you actually done about it?

options.text: Real work: counseling, honest conversations, spiritual processing. The wound still shaped me, but it no longer runs my decisions

genderInsight.male: Pursuing real healing — counseling, honest conversations, spiritual processing — is a choice many men never make. Your willingness to face pain rather than bury it makes you safer to love.
genderInsight.female: Intentional healing work shows you're not just surviving your past but transforming it. Your future husband benefits from a woman who has faced her wounds head-on.

options.text: Trusted people and prayer have helped. The wound is healing, but structured professional work has not been part of it yet

genderInsight.male: Informal processing with trusted people is valuable, but men often stop here — talking about the wound without the structured work that actually rewires the response. Consider whether talking has become a substitute for changing.
genderInsight.female: Community processing is powerful. The growth edge is moving from talking about the wound to structured work that changes how it controls your reactions in real-time.

options.text: I know it is there but I have mostly dealt with it by moving forward. I do not like revisiting painful things

genderInsight.male: Moving on without processing is the classic male approach to emotional wounds — 'it's in the past.' But unprocessed wounds don't stay in the past. They show up as anger, distance, or shutdown in your closest relationships.
genderInsight.female: Moving forward without looking back feels like strength but leaves the wound intact underneath. In marriage, unprocessed pain surfaces in unexpected ways — triggers, walls, and unexplained reactions.

options.text: Nothing, honestly. It stays underground until something forces it to the surface, and then it surprises even me

genderInsight.male: An untouched wound in a man is a time bomb in a marriage. It will surface when your wife least expects it — usually in conflict, intimacy, or moments of vulnerability. Address it now.
genderInsight.female: A wound you've never addressed doesn't stay quiet — it shapes your choices, your reactions, and your capacity for intimacy. In marriage, it will find its way to the surface.

questions.text: You have a packed week: work deadlines, personal goals, social commitments. Your partner (or someone close) says they need quality time with you. What do you do?

options.text: I rearrange something. They matter more than a packed schedule, and I make sure they know that

genderInsight.male: Rearranging your schedule for a partner shows that your relationship isn't just something you fit in around your real life. Many men keep partners in a separate compartment — this integration is healthy.
genderInsight.female: Making room for your partner when life is full shows relational maturity. Women sometimes over-accommodate here — make sure this priority-setting goes both ways.

options.text: Time gets squeezed in, but my mind would be elsewhere: physically present, mentally running through my to-do list

genderInsight.male: Present but distracted is a common male pattern — physically there but mentally elsewhere. Your partner will feel the difference between your body in the room and your attention in the conversation.
genderInsight.female: Squeezing in time while mentally elsewhere is common when life is full. Notice whether 'being there' actually means being present, or just being physically available.

options.text: An honest explanation that this week will not work, with a promise to make it up later that may or may not happen

genderInsight.male: Promising later but not now is a pattern that teaches your partner they're not a priority. Men often believe 'next week' is a reasonable answer — but your partner hears 'you're not important enough for today.'
genderInsight.female: Deferring connection to a future that rarely comes teaches your partner to stop asking. Marriage is built in the daily moments, not the someday promises.

options.text: I would feel frustrated by the request. I am already stretched thin and adding one more thing feels like pressure

genderInsight.male: If a partner's need for time feels like another demand on your overloaded life, relationships will always feel like obligations rather than investments. This mindset shift is crucial before marriage.
genderInsight.female: Feeling frustrated by a partner's needs suggests your capacity for relational investment is strained. Marriage will ask this of you every week — building capacity now prevents resentment later.

questions.text: You are offered an exciting career opportunity that would require you to move to a new city. If you were in a serious relationship, how would you approach this decision?

options.text: I would pray about it and discuss it deeply with my partner. This is a decision we would need to make together

genderInsight.male: Collaborative decision-making is a sign of partnership readiness. Many men default to deciding first and informing second — your instinct toward shared discernment shows you understand covenant.
genderInsight.female: Including your partner in major decisions from the beginning protects the partnership. Many women either defer entirely or decide independently — your collaborative instinct is the healthiest path.

options.text: Think it through first, then present my reasoning. My partner's input matters, but I would come to the table with a direction already in mind

genderInsight.male: Thinking it through alone first is natural for men — but notice the assumption: that your reasoning comes first and her input comes second. In marriage, the order matters.
genderInsight.female: Independent thinking followed by informing is efficient but can make your partner feel consulted rather than included. The difference matters in how valued they feel.

options.text: I would probably know what I want to do already, but I would feel conflicted about how my partner fits into it
options.outcomeLabel: decides alone, expects partner to adjust

genderInsight.male: Deciding alone and expecting your partner to adjust is a leadership failure disguised as decisiveness. In marriage, decisions made without your wife are decisions that undermine her trust.
genderInsight.female: If you already know what you want and your partner's role is to adjust, you're not in a partnership — you're in a management structure. Marriage requires genuine shared decision-making.

options.text: Paralysis. Big decisions that affect someone else lock me up. The weight of getting it wrong feels crushing

genderInsight.male: Decision paralysis under relational pressure suggests you need to build confidence in navigating competing priorities. Marriage requires constant joint decision-making — avoidance isn't an option.
genderInsight.female: If big decisions paralyze you when someone else's feelings are involved, you may be carrying a fear of disappointing others. In marriage, decisions must be made — sometimes imperfectly.

questions.text: You and your future spouse have your first real fight: raised voices, tears, strong emotions. In the aftermath, what would your instinctive pattern be?

options.text: Restless until it is resolved. Unfinished conflict sits in my chest and I would need to talk through it as soon as possible
options.outcomeLabel: needs to fix it fast, may rush partner

genderInsight.male: Needing to fix it immediately is common in men and often feels like care — but can overwhelm a partner who needs space first. Your instinct is good; your timing may need adjustment.
genderInsight.female: Wanting to resolve tension quickly comes from a good place, but can feel like pressure to a partner who processes differently. Learning to give space before repair is a growth edge.

options.text: I would give us both space to cool down, then come back to repair. I have learned that time helps before talking
options.outcomeLabel: gives space then comes back to repair

genderInsight.male: Space then repair is the most relationally intelligent post-fight pattern. Many men either rush to fix or withdraw permanently — your ability to do both in sequence is genuinely mature.
genderInsight.female: Giving space and then initiating repair shows you can manage your own anxiety while staying committed to connection. This is exactly what healthy marriage repair looks like.

options.text: Withdrawal and waiting: pulling back until they come to me, because something in me says the one who reaches out first loses
options.outcomeLabel: waits them out, refuses to go first

genderInsight.male: Withdrawing and waiting for them to come to you is a passive-aggressive pattern many men learned from watching their fathers. It shifts the repair burden entirely onto your partner.
genderInsight.female: Waiting for them to make the first move after a fight often comes from a belief that whoever apologizes first 'loses.' In marriage, the person who reaches out first shows the most courage.

options.text: I would feel terrified. Big fights remind me of something from my past and I might emotionally spiral

genderInsight.male: If conflict triggers old trauma, your body is running a program from childhood, not from the present relationship. Addressing the root — likely through therapy — changes everything.
genderInsight.female: When fights activate past pain rather than present-moment responses, your nervous system is stuck in an old story. Trauma-informed work can untangle your past from your future.

questions.text: You go through a season where nothing makes sense: a deep disappointment, an unanswered prayer, a loss that shakes you. What happens to your faith during that season?

options.text: My faith deepens. Suffering draws me closer to God even when I do not understand what He is doing

genderInsight.male: Faith that deepens under suffering — not just survives it — makes a man spiritually safe for a wife to follow into hard seasons. She needs to know your faith holds when the answers don't come.
genderInsight.female: Suffering that draws you closer to God rather than away shows a faith that functions under real-world conditions. Your future husband needs a wife whose faith doesn't collapse when life does.

options.text: I wrestle honestly with God. I bring my doubt and anger to Him rather than walking away, even when it is messy

genderInsight.male: A man with visible, consistent faith creates spiritual safety in a home. This isn't about perfection — it's about rhythm and authenticity.
genderInsight.female: Your consistent faith practice shows that your spiritual life is integrated, not compartmentalized. This will anchor a future marriage.

options.text: I drift. I stop praying, stop showing up, and only come back when the storm passes

genderInsight.male: Drifting from faith during hardship means your spiritual life is a fair-weather practice. Marriage will bring storms. A wife needs to know you'll turn toward God together, not disappear spiritually when it gets hard.
genderInsight.female: Stopping prayer and pulling away during hard seasons means faith is something you do when life is manageable, not a foundation for when it isn't. Marriage stress-tests everything — including this.

options.text: I question everything. Hard seasons make me wonder if God is real, good, or paying attention at all

genderInsight.male: Suffering that makes you question God's existence or goodness is an honest crisis — but it means your faith hasn't been tested and refined yet. A wife who looks to you for spiritual direction during crisis needs a faith that's been through fire.
genderInsight.female: If suffering shakes your entire belief system, your faith foundation hasn't yet been pressure-tested. This doesn't mean your faith isn't real — it means it needs deepening before it can bear the weight of marriage.
